Others say that refill stations are only convenient for people who work or travel in the city centre; those living in distant suburbs may still find it easier to buy a bottle. For the habit to change, therefore, the stations must be almost everywhere a person goes: stations, parks, schools, offices and bus stops.

That is a practical challenge, but hardly an impossible one. The real test is not whether people approve of free water in theory, but whether a refill is easier than a purchase. Where that is true, the old habit tends to disappear.

questions.q: What change does the author describe at the beginning of the passage?
options: Bottled water has lost its status as the natural choice.
Bottled water has become more expensive than ever.
Tap water has disappeared from supermarket shelves.
Restaurants have stopped serving water to customers.
questions.explain: 首段说二十年前瓶装水似乎是未来，如今城市安装公共直饮点、发放可重复使用的水瓶，说明它不再是默认选择，故选 A。

questions.q: What do supporters of refill stations argue?
options: Bottled water contains too much sugar.
Refill stations should be run by the government.
Bottled water costs more and often tastes no better.
Reusable bottles are easier to carry than plastic ones.
questions.explain: 第二段说支持者指出自来水比瓶装水便宜得多，并质疑口感差异是否真有广告说的那么大，盲测中许多人分辨不出，故选 C。

questions.q: What is the main challenge facing the refill movement?
options: Lack of support from city governments.
Making refill stations convenient for everyone.
The high cost of building the stations.
A shortage of clean water in big cities.
questions.explain: 第三、四段说真正的挑战是让直饮点几乎出现在人们去的所有地方，使接水比买水更方便，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2025年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Ask people to describe their ideal day and few will mention boredom. We treat it as a failure of planning, something to be removed with a phone, a game or another cup of coffee. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that boredom is not an enemy at all. It may even be useful.

In a well-known experiment, volunteers were asked to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory. Afterwards, they were given a test of creativity: they had to suggest as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The bored group produced far more original ideas than a control group who had spent the same time doing something pleasant. The researchers believe that when the mind is under-stimulated, it starts to search for new directions, connecting memories and ideas in ways that a busy mind cannot.

Boredom also sends a signal. Just as hunger tells us to eat, boredom tells us that what we are doing is not meaningful, and it pushes us to change something: to call a friend, start a project or take a walk. People who never allow themselves to be bored may lose that signal, and with it the chance to notice what really matters to them.

The modern world, however, makes boredom almost impossible. Every spare minute can be filled with messages, videos and shopping. Some teachers therefore ask students to leave their phones at home for a day, and many report that the first hours are uncomfortable but that conversations become longer and homework gets finished faster. Perhaps the skill we need most is not entertainment, but the ability to sit with an empty moment and see what it brings.

questions.q: What do many psychologists now believe about boredom?
options: It is mainly caused by poor planning.
It can be valuable to the mind.
It should be treated with coffee.
It is a sign of mental illness.
questions.explain: 第一段说越来越多心理学家认为无聊根本不是敌人，甚至可能有用，故选 B。

questions.q: What did the telephone-directory experiment find?
options: Bored people disliked the creativity test.
The control group was more creative.
Boredom made people feel tired quickly.
Bored people produced more original ideas.
questions.explain: 第二段说抄号码簿而无聊的一组在随后的创造力测试中提出的原创想法远多于对照组，故选 D。

questions.q: What does the author compare boredom to?
options: A game played on a phone.
A failure of daily planning.
A signal such as hunger.
A cup of coffee in the morning.
questions.explain: 第三段把无聊比作饥饿：饥饿提醒我们进食，无聊提醒我们正在做的事没有意义，故选 C。

questions.q: What do some teachers ask their students to do?
options: Leave their phones at home for a day.
Spend more time playing computer games.
Copy numbers from a directory every day.
Stop doing homework in the evening.
questions.explain: 最后一段说一些老师要求学生一整天把手机留在家里，学生反映最初不适应，但交谈变长、作业完成得更快，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2025年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Street food is one of the joys of city life: a hot bowl of noodles, a paper cone of fried chicken or a warm pancake eaten while walking. For many people it is also cheaper than a restaurant, and for small business owners it offers a way to start trading with very little capital. For a visitor, it is also the quickest way to taste what a city really eats.

Yet street food has long had a reputation problem. Because stalls are small and often temporary, health inspectors find it difficult to check every one, and customers cannot see what happens behind the counter. In some cities, the answer has been to ban street selling altogether, but this usually drives vendors into less visible places, where conditions may be even worse.

A number of cities are now trying a different approach. Instead of closing markets, they are organised. Vendors are given a fixed pitch with clean water and rubbish collection, in exchange for paying a small fee and following basic rules such as storing food at the correct temperature and covering it. Some markets train their own members and publish inspection results on a notice board, so that a stall that loses customers will think twice about food safety.

The early results are positive. In one city, complaints about food safety fell by half after the first year, while the number of stalls rose, which suggests that customers and sellers both benefit. The lesson is that street food does not have to choose between charm and hygiene. With a little organisation, a city can keep its lively streets and its safe meals.

questions.q: What advantage of street food does the author mention?
options: It requires very little money to start.
It always tastes better than restaurant food.
It is only sold late at night.
It is easy for inspectors to check.
questions.explain: 第一段说对小微经营者而言，街头小吃让他们能用很少的本钱开始做生意，故选 A。

questions.q: What usually happens when cities ban street selling?
options: Street food becomes much safer.
Vendors move to less visible places.
Prices fall in the city centre.
Customers stop eating street food.
questions.explain: 第二段说全面禁止通常把摊贩逼到更不显眼的地方，那里的卫生条件可能更差，故选 B。

questions.q: What does the new approach give vendors?
options: Free advertising on local radio.
A larger restaurant in the city centre.
A fixed pitch with clean water and rubbish collection.
Tax-free income for the first year.
questions.explain: 第三段说城市给摊贩固定摊位、提供清洁用水和垃圾清运，条件是交纳少量费用并遵守基本规则，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2025年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
At home, a typical student may be reading a course text, replying to messages and half-watching a video, all at the same time. People who do this often describe themselves as good at multitasking. Research tells a different story. When the brain switches between two tasks, it does not process both at once; it moves its attention from one to the other, and each switch costs a little time. The effect is small when switches are rare, but it adds up when messages arrive every few minutes.

In one study, students were asked to read a chapter while receiving short messages. Compared with a quiet group, they took about a quarter longer to finish and later remembered less of what they had read. Another line of research found that students who used their phones during lectures took notes of a lower quality and were more likely to miss the connection between ideas.

There is a trap here. Because messages are brief, students feel that they have lost only a few seconds. In fact, they must rebuild their understanding of the text each time they return to it, and that rebuilding is the expensive part. Some researchers call this attention residue: part of the mind remains on the conversation even after the phone is put away.

Experiments with simpler solutions have been encouraging. Students who left their phones in another room, or who turned off notifications for a single hour, reported no great difficulty and finished their work faster. The lesson is not that technology is harmful, but that attention is limited. It deserves the same care that we give to any other valuable resource.

questions.q: What do people who multitask often believe about themselves?
options: They finish every task more quickly.
They are good at handling several tasks at once.
They remember more than other people.
They need fewer breaks than others.
questions.explain: 第一段说同时做几件事的人常自称擅长多任务处理，研究却给出不同结论，故选 B。

questions.q: What did the study on reading and messages find?
options: Short messages improved students' memory of the text.
Quiet students read more slowly than others.
Students ignored most of the messages they received.
Students took longer to finish and remembered less.
questions.explain: 第二段说边读边收短信的一组比安静组多花约四分之一时间，且记住的内容更少，故选 D。

questions.q: What does attention residue mean?
options: The tiredness caused by long hours of reading.
The habit of checking messages late at night.
Part of the mind staying on a previous task.
A technique for taking better notes in class.
questions.explain: 第三段把 attention residue 解释为放下手机后仍有一部分注意力留在刚才的对话上，故选 C。

questions.q: What solution does the text suggest?
options: Keep phones away or turn off notifications.
Stop using technology for studying entirely.
Study only in the early morning.
Read the same chapter twice every day.
questions.explain: 最后一段说把手机放到另一个房间或关闭一小时通知，学生并没有太大困难，反而更快完成任务，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2025年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Ask an urban planner what makes a neighbourhood pleasant, and the answer is often a single number: fifteen. The idea of the fifteen-minute city is that people should be able to reach most of what they need, such as shops, schools, a clinic, a park and a place to meet friends, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. The concept is not new; many older towns grew up this way before cars became common. What is new is how seriously some cities now take it when planning new districts.

The benefits sound obvious, but they are worth stating. Streets with fewer cars are quieter and safer, and children who can walk to school are healthier than those who are driven. Small local shops survive when residents pass them daily, and older people who can reach a clinic on foot keep their independence longer. The environment gains too: short car journeys are the most polluting, so replacing them with walking or cycling cuts both emissions and noise.

Bringing the idea to an existing city is harder. Shops may have already moved to large shopping centres on the edge of town, and office workers may live far from their workplaces. Planners therefore talk about a network of local centres rather than a single perfect district: a few shops here, a clinic there, a good bus link between them. The aim is to make the ordinary journey to the shop or the school one that a person can imagine walking, rather than one that requires a car key.

Cities that have tried it report that the change is gradual. People do not switch to walking because a plan tells them to; they switch because the walk is pleasant, safe and convenient. Design, in the end, shapes habit.

questions.q: What is the fifteen-minute city?
options: A city where daily needs are within a short walk or cycle.
A city with fifteen parks in every district.
A city where trains arrive every fifteen minutes.
A city that bans cars from its centre completely.
questions.explain: 第一段说十五分钟城市指步行或骑车一刻钟内能到达商店、学校、诊所和公园等日常所需之处，故选 A。

questions.q: Which benefit of the idea is mentioned in the passage?
options: Property prices fall in local areas.
Local shops keep more customers.
People spend less time at home.
Public transport becomes free of charge.
questions.explain: 第二段说居民每天经过，小店铺才得以存活，即本地商店能留住更多顾客，故选 B。

questions.q: Why is the idea hard to apply to existing cities?
options: Residents refuse to walk anywhere.
There are not enough urban planners.
Shops and jobs are often located far away.
Walking is impossible in cold weather.
questions.explain: 第三段说商店可能已搬到城郊的大型购物中心，上班族也可能住得很远，因此规划者提出本地中心网络，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1

items.passage:
Three years ago, the science magazine of a small university nearly closed. Its editor had graduated, the printer had raised its prices, and only four students remained on the team. Rather than let the magazine disappear, the four decided to change it. They stopped printing long articles written by professors and began to publish short pieces by undergraduates about research taking place on campus. The first issue of the new format was thirty pages long and included an interview with a student who had spent the summer counting insects in a city park.
The change worked. Readers said they finally understood what their classmates were working on, and students who had never written anything for a general audience discovered that explaining their subject was harder than they had imagined. A chemistry student described how a paragraph about her project went through five drafts before her flatmate could follow it. That experience, she said, was more useful than any writing course.
The magazine is now published twice a term, with a print run of eight hundred copies, and it has a small budget from the student union. The editor is careful not to call it a research journal. Its purpose, she says, is not to record science but to start conversations: a reader who finishes an article should have a question to ask the person sitting next to them.
Not every issue succeeds. Some topics attract few readers, and the team has learned to accept that. What matters is that a magazine which almost closed now has a waiting list of students who want to write for it, and that the science on campus is no longer invisible.

questions.q: What caused the science magazine to nearly close?
options: Professors stopped writing for it.
It lost its editor and faced higher printing costs.
The student union cut its budget.
Readers complained about its length.
questions.explain: 第一段说 Its editor had graduated, the printer had raised its prices, and only four students remained，即编辑毕业、印刷涨价、人手只剩四人，故选 B。

questions.q: What did the team change about the magazine?
options: They began publishing short articles by undergraduates about campus research.
They moved the magazine online.
They invited professors to write longer articles.
They started a second journal.
questions.explain: 第一段说 They stopped printing long articles written by professors and began to publish short pieces by undergraduates about research taking place on campus，故选 A。

options: How to run a laboratory experiment.

How to become an editor.

questions.q: What does the editor say is the purpose of the magazine?
options: To record scientific results.

items.passage:
Every autumn, the international office at a British university runs a short course that has nothing to do with engineering or literature. It is called Academic Etiquette, and its purpose is to explain the unwritten rules of university life: how to address a professor, how to join a discussion without interrupting, and how to write an email that will actually be answered.
The email lesson is the most popular. Students bring messages they have already sent, and the class reads them together. Two versions appear again and again. One begins with no greeting and no subject line and asks five questions at once. The other begins with a long apology for troubling the professor, followed by a paragraph about the student's entire academic history, before the real request appears in the final line. Neither is likely to receive a quick reply.
The teacher offers a simple structure: a subject line that says exactly what the message is about, a brief greeting, the request in the first two sentences, and a closing that thanks the reader for their time. She also reminds students that professors receive hundreds of messages a week, and that a short, clear email is a sign of respect rather than a sign of laziness.
At the end of the course, students are asked to rewrite one of their own messages. The improvement is usually obvious. But the teacher insists that the deeper lesson is not about language. It is about understanding that academic life has its own culture, with habits and expectations that nobody explains in class. Learning to read that culture, she says, is part of learning the subject itself.

questions.q: What is the Academic Etiquette course mainly about?
options: Teaching international students English grammar.
Helping students pass their final exams.
Explaining the unwritten rules of university life.
Training professors to write better emails.
questions.explain: 第一段说 its purpose is to explain the unwritten rules of university life，并列举称呼教授、加入讨论、写邮件等，故选 C。

questions.q: What do the two common email versions share?
options: Both make the real request hard to find.
Both begin with a clear subject line.
Both are written in very short sentences.
Both are sent to the wrong professor.
questions.explain: 第二段说一种邮件没有称呼和主题、一口气问五个问题，另一种先长篇道歉、把真正的请求放到最后一句，共同点是请求很难被找到，故选 A。

questions.q: What does the teacher believe is the deeper lesson?
options: Professors should reply to emails faster.
Language is not important in academic emails.
Students should stop asking so many questions.
Understanding academic culture is part of learning a subject.
questions.explain: 末段说 the deeper lesson is not about language，而是理解 academic life has its own culture，学会读懂这种文化本身就是学习这门学科的一部分，故选 D。

items.passage: When physicians describe the placebo effect, they usually mean the improvement patients experience after receiving an inactive treatment simply because they expect to feel better. For decades, medical students were taught that this was a nuisance, a statistical noise that made trials harder to interpret. More recent research has complicated that view. Brain scans show that when patients believe a painkiller has been given, the brain releases its own natural pain-relieving chemicals. In other words, expectation is not merely a state of mind; it produces measurable physical changes. The finding has practical consequences. Trials must now be designed so that neither patients nor doctors know who is receiving the real drug, since even a doctor's optimism can influence the result. Some researchers go further and argue that the effect should be used rather than eliminated: if a doctor's manner and a patient's expectations can improve outcomes, then those aspects of care deserve as much attention as the prescription itself. Critics warn that this reasoning can be taken too far, and that no placebo has ever cured a broken bone. Both sides agree, however, that the mind's influence on the body is far from imaginary.

questions.q: How was the placebo effect traditionally regarded in medical education?
options: As a valuable treatment.
As a nuisance in trials.
As proof of drug effectiveness.
As a psychological cure.
questions.explain: 第一段说 medical students were taught that this was a nuisance, a statistical noise，即传统上安慰剂效应被视为试验中的干扰因素，故选 B。

questions.q: What do brain scans show about expectation?
options: It produces measurable physical changes.
It has no effect on the body.
It reduces the need for painkillers.
It affects only emotional states.
questions.explain: 第二段说 expectation is not merely a state of mind; it produces measurable physical changes，即期待会产生可测量的生理变化，故选 A。

questions.q: Why must trials be designed as double-blind?
options: To reduce the cost of research.
Because a doctor's optimism may influence the result.
Because patients refuse to take real drugs.
To speed up the approval process.
questions.explain: 第三段说 Trials must now be designed so that neither patients nor doctors know who is receiving the real drug, since even a doctor's optimism can influence the result，故选 B。

questions.q: What is the critics' concern?
options: The effect has never been observed.
The reasoning can be carried too far.
Doctors ignore patients' expectations.
Trials are no longer reliable.
questions.explain: 第四段说 Critics warn that this reasoning can be taken too far, and that no placebo has ever cured a broken bone，即批评者担心这种推理被推得过远，故选 B。

items.passage: For anyone who has tried to sleep on a plane, the appeal of the night train is obvious. Yet for years, Europe's sleeper services seemed to be disappearing: routes were cut, carriages aged, and cheap short-haul flights took most of the passengers. Recently the trend has reversed. Several governments have announced new sleeper routes, and a number of private companies are buying second-hand carriages to compete with the state railways. The revival owes much to climate policy: a train journey from Paris to Vienna produces a small fraction of the emissions of the equivalent flight. But the operators insist that passengers are not only motivated by green concerns. Travelling overnight saves the cost of a hotel room and an entire day of travelling, which matters to business travellers and families alike. Difficulties remain. Sleeper trains are expensive to run, and crossing borders still involves paperwork and different signalling systems. Even so, tickets for many new routes sell out within days of going on sale, suggesting that demand, at least, is not a problem.

Governments banned sleeper services.
Tickets cost too much.

items.passage: Journal editors decide what gets published and what doesn’t, affecting the careers of other academics and influencing the direction that a field takes. You’d hope, then, that journals would do everything they can to establish a diverse editorial board, reflecting a variety of voices, experiences, and identities. The team finds that the majority of editors in top psychology and neuroscience journals are male and based in the United States: a situation that may be amplifying existing gender inequalities in the field and influencing the kind of research that gets published. Men were found to account for 60% of the editors of psychology journals. There were significantly more male than female editors at each level of seniority, and men made up the majority of editors in over three quarters of the journals. Crucially, the proportion of female editors was significantly lower than the overall proportion of women psychology researchers. The differences were even starker in the neuroscience journals: 70% of editors were male, and men held the majority of editorial positions in 88% of journals. In this case, the proportion of female editors was not reveals enduring gender disparities in the field more broadly. Based on their results, the team concludes that “the ideas, values and decision-making biases of men are overrepresented Gender inequality in science is often attributed to the fact that senior academics are more likely to be male, because historically science was male-dominated: it’s argued that as time goes on and more women rise psychology journals tended to be held disproportionately by men, despite the fact that there are actually more female than male junior psychology faculty. items.passage: Why are we so worried about our careers? Partly it’s to do with money, but there’s a psychological aspect to our fears as well. We worry because we suspect — not wrongly — that the world is full of a frightening sort of person ready to judge us ruthlessly and swiftly: a person we can call a snob. A snob is anyone who takes a relatively small part of us and uses it to come to a rigid conclusion about how much of their attention we deserve. In the past, that might be your ancestry and royal connections. Nowadays, the snob cares about one thing only: what you do for a living. This explains why the first question we will be asked in social context is “What do do?” and according to how we answer, snobs will either welcome us with broad smiles, or leave us in the cold. And that is why we are fired up by such a desperate urge to achieve and impress. Sometimes our behaviour is mistaken for greed and vanity, but it is more than this. A lot of our interest in fancy cars, jobs and houses has nothing to do with materialism. It has to do with a hunger for the respect and esteem that is only available in our societies through the acquisition of material goods. It isn’t the goods themselves we seek, it is gain through shouldn’t condemn them for their greed, we should pity them for the intensity of their need for love from the world. valuable. The snobs are brutally misguided and slavish in their beliefs about how the superior individuals can be identified. For snobs, it is the already acclaimed and already successful who are the only ones worthy of respect. There is no room in their timid regimented minds to imagine that someone might be clever, kind or good — and yet having as yet discovered no obvious outlet. items.title: The Case for Productive Struggle
items.passage:
For generations, good teaching was easy to recognize: a knowledgeable instructor delivered clear explanations while students listened and took notes. Clarity still matters, but research on learning has gradually shifted attention from what students hear to what they do. A growing number of educators now argue that the most durable learning often begins where understanding breaks down.

The idea is usually described as productive struggle. When learners wrestle with a problem before being shown the solution, they must retrieve what they already know, notice gaps, and build connections between ideas. These mental operations feel effortful, and the effort is precisely the point. Material that arrives too smoothly can create a pleasant illusion of competence that fades quickly once the lesson ends.

This does not mean abandoning guidance. Novices can flounder when a task is too open-ended, and frustration that turns into hopelessness teaches nothing. The art lies in calibration: problems should sit just beyond what students can currently manage alone, yet within reach with hints, peer discussion, or a well-timed question. Teachers therefore need to resist the urge to rescue learners at the first sign of difficulty.

Assessment practices complicate matters. Grades tend to reward quick correct answers, which encourages students to hide confusion rather than explore it. Some schools now separate the grade for a final product from the feedback given during practice, so that mistakes made while rehearsing carry no penalty. The aim is to make experimentation feel safe.

None of this is an argument for making school needlessly hard. Struggle is productive only when it is purposeful, when learners understand why a task is worth the discomfort, and when they receive feedback soon enough to adjust. Encouraged in that way, students may leave school not merely with facts in hand but with the confidence to approach unfamiliar problems.

questions.q: What shift in emphasis does the author describe in the first paragraph?
options: From clear explanations to the notes students take during lessons
From what students hear to what students actually do
From difficult problems to easy classroom exercises
From teacher training to the design of examination papers
questions.explain: 第一段明确指出研究重心已从“学生听到什么”转向“学生做什么”，故选第二项。第一项仍停留在听讲层面，第三、四项文中均未提及。

teachers believing that their explanations are more effective than they are
the confidence that grows from solving a genuinely difficult problem

questions.explain: 该短语承接上文“材料来得太顺”，指学生因学习过程毫不费力而高估自己的掌握程度。第二项偷换主体，第三项与“困难才有价值”的论点相反，第四项在文中指反馈，与错觉无关。

items.title: The Cost of Frictionless Technology
items.passage:
Modern digital tools are designed to remove friction. Maps calculate routes, keyboards correct our spelling, and platforms decide which films we might enjoy. Each small convenience is genuinely welcome, and few users would willingly return to a world of paper maps and manual indexes. Yet the smoothness of these systems invites a question that designers rarely address: what happens to the abilities we stop using?

Skills tend to fade when they are never exercised. Someone who always follows a navigation prompt may gradually lose the habit of building a mental map of a city, and a student who leans on automatic correction may become less certain about spelling without assistance. This is not nostalgia for older tools. It is a familiar pattern: competence that is outsourced to a device tends to remain undeveloped or quietly decline.

The effects are uneven. A tool that handles routine work can free attention for more demanding tasks, and few people would argue that mental arithmetic should compete with a spreadsheet. The concern arises when reliance becomes invisible. When people can no longer notice that a decision has been made for them, or explain why a recommendation appeared, they lose the ability to question the system and to correct it when it fails.

Designers have begun to respond with tools that invite engagement rather than replace it. Some navigation applications, for instance, offer a broader view before zooming in, so users still form a rough sense of direction. Others explain the reason behind a suggestion. The common principle is to leave the user with a role, however small, in the process.

What matters, then, is not whether we use intelligent tools but how we use them. Convenience is not a vice, and no one should be asked to perform every task unaided. But a useful test is to ask what a tool is doing for us and what it may be doing instead of us. Tools that keep that distinction visible are more likely to remain servants rather than substitutes.

questions.q: What does the author acknowledge about digital convenience in the first paragraph?
options: It is rarely welcomed by ordinary users
It is genuinely useful, and few people would give it up

questions.explain: 首段承认每种便利都“确实受欢迎”，且很少有人愿意回到纸质地图的时代，故选第二项。第一项与原文相反，第三项文中未提年龄差异，第四项用“all”过度绝对。

items.title: The Quiet Return of Repair
items.passage:
Not long ago, throwing away a broken object was a practical decision. A faulty kettle or a torn jacket often cost less to replace than to mend, and repair services were scarce in many neighborhoods. In recent years, however, a counter-movement has taken shape, driven less by nostalgia than by a simple calculation: the things we discard carry materials, energy, and labor that are expensive to replace.

Repair events and community workshops have appeared in many towns, where volunteers help visitors fix small appliances, bicycles, and clothing. Their appeal lies partly in money saved, but also in the experience itself. A person who opens a device and finds a loose connection learns that the object is not a mysterious sealed box. That shift in perception can change how people shop, and how long they keep what they buy.

Manufacturers influence this more than any campaign. Products that can be opened, that share standard parts, and that come with spare components are far easier to repair. Some companies have begun to publish manuals and sell parts, partly in response to consumer pressure, partly because durable products can build loyalty. The trend is uneven, and sealed designs remain common, but the direction of the conversation has changed.

Repair culture also raises awkward questions. Some fixes are genuinely risky, particularly when they involve electricity, gas, or safety equipment, and a well-meaning attempt can create a new hazard. There is also the matter of time: many people would rather buy a new item than spend an afternoon learning to mend an old one. Campaigns that ignore these realities tend to preach to the converted.

The most persuasive argument for repair may be the least dramatic. It is not that everyone should become a technician, but that keeping some objects in use should be an ordinary option rather than an unusual act. When spare parts, clear instructions, and skilled help are within reach, repair stops being a hobby for enthusiasts and becomes what it once was: a normal part of owning things.

questions.q: What reason does the author give for the growth of repair culture?
options: A widespread longing for the habits of an earlier age

The growing difficulty of finding new products to buy
questions.explain: 首段指出这场运动更多出于“计算”而非怀旧：被丢弃的物品内含昂贵的材料、能源与劳动，故选第三项。第一项恰好被作者否定，第二、四项文中无据。

questions.explain: 第二段说打开设备的人会发现物件并非神秘的黑箱，这种认知转变会影响购买习惯，故第一项正确。第二项与原文相反，第三项无据，第四项过度概括，文中也承认部分维修有风险。

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Sitting Still
items.passage:
For most of human history, physical activity was not something people scheduled. It was built into the shape of daily life: walking to collect water, carrying firewood, working land. Modern routines are different. Many people can now pass an entire working day without standing for more than a few minutes, and the body was never designed for that kind of stillness.

The problem is not simply a lack of formal exercise. Someone may run in the morning and still spend most of the day seated, and researchers increasingly argue that long, uninterrupted sitting has effects of its own. Muscles that remain idle for hours process fuel differently, and the circulation of blood slows. These changes are subtle, which is exactly why they are easy to ignore.

The encouraging news is that small interruptions appear to matter. Getting up to fill a glass of water, taking a short walk during a phone call, or simply standing while reading can break up long periods of stillness. The goal is not a workout; it is to reset the body's pattern. Individuals who build such moments into their routines often report that the habit is easier to sustain than a formal exercise plan.

Workplaces shape this behavior more than willpower does. When stairs are more visible than lifts, when meetings are sometimes held on foot, and when short breaks are treated as normal rather than as laziness, movement becomes the path of least resistance. Culture matters too: employees who leave their desks may be judged as uncommitted unless the organization makes clear that it expects them to move.

None of this dismisses the value of planned exercise, which remains important for strength, endurance, and mood. But it does suggest that the question "Did I work out today?" is too narrow. How long we sit without interruption, and how readily our surroundings let us move, may matter as much as the hours we spend in a gym. The remedy is partly personal and partly collective.

questions.q: What does the author say about physical activity in the past?
options: It was something people deliberately scheduled each week
It was built into the ordinary pattern of daily life
It was rare because most work required little movement
It was mainly performed in dedicated exercise spaces
questions.explain: 首段说过去的体力活动并非刻意安排，而是融入日常：取水、搬柴、耕地，故选第二项。第一项与原文相反，第三项无据，第四项是现代健身房的模式而非过去。

medically serious and painful

questions.explain: 下文说这些变化“正因为细微才容易被忽视”，故指“轻微而不易察觉”。第一项与“易被忽略”矛盾，第二项文中未提疼痛，第四项无依据。

questions.q: What are the small interruptions in paragraph 3 meant to do?
options: Break up long periods of inactivity
Replace a formal exercise plan completely

questions.explain: 第三段说明这些小动作的目的是“打断长时间的静止”，而非进行锻炼，故选第一项。第二项与“目标不是锻炼”不符，第三项属于有计划的运动，第四项文中未提。

items.title: Rethinking the Working Week
items.passage:
The idea of a shorter working week has moved from the margins of debate into ordinary conversation. Advocates argue that many office jobs contain hours of low-value activity, and that compressing the week could sharpen focus. Critics reply that the notion is unrealistic for hospitals, factories, and shops, where work must be done at particular times. Both sides have a point, which is why the discussion is more interesting than it first appears.

Much of the evidence about shorter schedules comes from workplaces that chose to experiment, so conclusions should be drawn carefully. A team that volunteers for a trial is not a typical sample, and the enthusiasm of a new arrangement can fade after the novelty passes. Even so, the basic lesson seems durable: when hours are shorter, people tend to protect them. Meetings shrink, interruptions are tolerated less readily, and work that once expanded to fill the day is completed in less time.

The arrangement suits some jobs far better than others. Knowledge work, which depends on concentration and creativity, may gain from a tight schedule. Care work, sales, and emergency services are different: coverage matters more than efficiency, and a shorter week usually means hiring more people rather than working differently. In those settings, the real question is not hours but staffing and pay.

There is also a fairness issue. If shorter weeks become a privilege of certain occupations, the gap between secure office jobs and shift work may widen. A serious policy would need to consider who bears the costs of change. Some experiments reduce hours without cutting pay, which is generous but hard to sustain across an entire economy. Others cut pay as well, which tends to be unpopular.

Perhaps the most useful outcome of the debate is not a fixed answer but a better question: which parts of the working day are genuinely productive, and which parts exist out of habit? Organizations that answer that honestly may find room for change even where a shortened week remains impractical.

questions.q: What is the critics' main objection to a shorter working week?
options: It would reduce pay for office employees
It is unrealistic where work must happen at set times
It would make employees less careful about quality
It suits hospitals but not other workplaces
questions.explain: 首段指出批评者认为对医院、工厂、商店而言不现实，因为这些地方的工作必须在特定时间完成，故选第二项。第一项是后文减薪方案的讨论，第三项无据，第四项把适用范围说反了。

questions.q: The word "durable" in paragraph 2 most nearly means
options: lasting and reliable
surprising and new
expensive to test
flexible in practice
questions.explain: 此处说即使样本有局限，“基本教训”似乎依然成立且持久，故为“经得起时间检验”。第一项最贴合；第二项与 novelty 的语境相反，第三、四项与语义无关。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what tends to happen when working hours are shortened?
options: Meetings multiply and take up more time
People become more protective of their time
Work expands to fill the shorter day
The quality of work falls sharply
questions.explain: 第二段说工时缩短后人们更倾向于守住时间：会议变短、更不容忍打断，故选第二项。第一、三项与原文相反，第四项文中未作此判断。

questions.q: Why does the author say the arrangement suits some jobs better than others?
options: Because knowledge workers refuse to work in teams
Because shift workers are paid more than office staff
Because in care work and emergency services, coverage matters more than efficiency
Because fewer people are needed in factories and shops
questions.explain: 第三段区分两类工作：知识型工作依赖专注与创造，而护理、销售、应急服务更看重覆盖，缩短工时往往需要增加人手，故选第三项。第一、二项文中无据，第四项与“需多招人”相反。

questions.q: What can be inferred about the author's attitude toward the debate?
options: The debate is largely meaningless because no answer is possible
Shorter weeks should be adopted everywhere at once
Office workers deserve privileges that others do not
The discussion is valuable because it clarifies which hours are truly productive
questions.explain: 末段说这场辩论最有价值的成果不是固定答案，而是更好的问题——哪些工时真正有产出，故第四项正确。第一项与作者“讨论很有意思”的态度相反，第二、三项都非作者主张。

items.title: Museums That Tell Stories
items.passage:
A museum is often imagined as a quiet hall of objects, each displayed behind glass. That image is not wrong, but it is incomplete. In practice, every exhibition makes choices: what to include, where to place it, and what to say about it. A single label can decide whether a visitor sees a pot as a technical achievement, a household tool, or a sign of trade with distant places.

In recent decades, many museums have become more openly storytelling institutions. Exhibitions are arranged to guide visitors through an argument, and digital guides, audio trails, and immersive rooms are used to provide context. The intention is generous: to make collections meaningful to people who arrive without specialist knowledge, and to show that objects were made and used by human beings.

Not everyone is persuaded. Some historians worry that a strong narrative can smooth over uncertainty, presenting as settled what is still debated. A story is easier to follow than a set of competing interpretations, and visitors may leave with confidence that experts do not share. Others argue that a museum should not pretend to be neutral, since its choices already express values.

The more interesting question is how to combine narrative with honesty. Curators who do it well make the process visible: they explain why an object matters, admit where evidence is thin, and show that collections themselves have histories, including the difficult ways in which some objects were acquired. Visitors respond well to this candor. Being trusted with complexity, it turns out, is more engaging than being told a tidy story.

Museums are not merely storehouses; they are places where a society decides what to remember and how to explain it to itself. That responsibility argues for imagination and care in equal measure. A good exhibition leaves visitors not with a finished message but with a question they did not have before they walked in.

questions.q: What does the author say about exhibition choices in the first paragraph?
options: They are neutral because museums avoid value judgments
Only the objects on display really matter
Decisions about inclusion and labels shape what visitors understand
Museums deliberately avoid explaining objects to visitors
questions.explain: 首段说每场展览都在做选择：展什么、放哪里、如何说明，一块标签就能决定观众如何理解一件器物，故选第三项。第一项与后文“选择本身已表达价值”矛盾，第二、四项与展签说明的例子相反。

questions.q: Why have many museums turned toward storytelling?
options: To attract specialist researchers rather than general visitors
To make collections meaningful to people without specialist knowledge
To reduce the cost of maintaining their buildings
To avoid taking any position on difficult subjects
questions.explain: 第二段明确说其用心是让没有专业背景的观众也能理解藏品，并展示器物由人制作和使用，故选第二项。第一项与“非专业观众”相反，第三项无据，第四项与后文“不必假装中立”相悖。

questions.q: The word "candor" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: a confident and forceful tone
careful avoidance of difficult topics
detailed visual decoration
frank honesty about what is known and unknown
questions.explain: 上文说策展人承认证据薄弱、说明藏品来历，下文说观众乐于被信任去面对复杂性，故指“坦率诚实”。第一项侧重语气，第二项与“承认薄弱”相反，第三项与语境无关。

questions.q: According to the author, how do visitors respond to complexity?
options: They engage with it when they are trusted to handle it
They prefer to be given a tidy message
They become confused and leave the museum
They reject any narrative offered by curators
questions.explain: 第四段末句说“被信任去面对复杂性，比被灌输一个整洁的故事更有吸引力”，故选第一项。第二项正是作者所否定的做法，第三项无据，第四项与观众“反响良好”相反。

questions.q: What can be inferred about a good exhibition from the last paragraph?
options: It answers every question a visitor might have
It avoids raising any question at all
It provokes new questions rather than delivering a finished message
It presents one settled interpretation of the past
questions.explain: 末段说好展览留给观众的不是完成的信息，而是一个此前没有的问题，故选第三项。第一、二项与“不是完成的信息”矛盾，第四项与全文倡导的诚实呈现分歧相反。

items.title: Science's Invisible Results
items.passage:
Scientific progress is usually described as a sequence of discoveries: a hypothesis is tested, a result is announced, and knowledge advances. This account is tidy but misleading. Most experiments do not produce a striking outcome, and many fail to support the idea that inspired them. Such results are essential, because they tell researchers which paths are worth abandoning, yet they are far less likely to be published or read.

The asymmetry has consequences. If journals prefer clear, positive findings, then the published record becomes a distorted sample of what was actually tried. Researchers may waste time repeating failures that were never reported, and readers may overestimate how consistent the evidence is. The problem is structural rather than a matter of individual dishonesty: careers depend on visible success, and invisible results do not build reputations.

Reformers have proposed several remedies. Some journals now accept studies on the basis of their methods, before the results are known, so that an unexciting outcome cannot be a reason for rejection. Others publish registered reports, in which the design is reviewed in advance, or offer formats devoted to negative results. Each approach has costs, particularly the extra work of reviewing a study twice.

Replication is the related issue. A single demonstration, however elegant, may reflect chance or an unnoticed factor. Confirmation by independent groups is what turns an interesting observation into a dependable one, but such work is often seen as unoriginal, and funding tends to favor novelty. The culture of science therefore rewards the very thing it claims to distrust: isolated, dramatic findings.

The deeper point concerns honesty about uncertainty. Science works not because its results are always right but because its errors can eventually be found. That requires a record that includes the failures as well as the successes. A field that publishes only its victories slowly loses the information it needs to test itself.

questions.q: What does the author say about the results of most experiments?
options: They are dramatic and immediately useful
They are never worth publishing at all
They are usually reported before they are checked
They are unremarkable or unsupportive of the original idea
questions.explain: 首段指出多数实验不会产生惊人结果，许多甚至不支持原来的设想，故选第四项。第一项与原文相反，第二项与“这些结果至关重要”矛盾，第三项讨论的是报道时机，文中未提。

questions.q: What does the author identify as the cause of the publication problem?
options: Structural incentives rather than individual dishonesty
Deliberate fraud committed by most researchers
A shortage of journals willing to publish results
A lack of public interest in scientific work
questions.explain: 第二段明确说问题在于结构性激励——职业发展依赖可见的成功，而非个人不诚实，故选第一项。第二项被原文直接排除，第三、四项文中未提及。

questions.q: The word "asymmetry" in paragraph 2 most probably refers to
options: disagreement among journals about standards
unequal funding between scientific fields
the gap between the work that is done and the work that is published
the balance between theory and experiment
questions.explain: 上文说大量未产生惊人结果的实验极少被发表，第二段随即讨论这种“做过的”与“发表的”之间的不对等，故选第三项。第一、二、四项均非该词所指。

questions.q: Why is replication described as being treated as unoriginal?
options: Because it always confirms earlier results
Because it is seen as unoriginal while funding favors novelty
Because it requires no funding at all
Because it is theoretically impossible to carry out
questions.explain: 第四段说重复验证常被视为缺乏新意，而经费更青睐新颖性，故选第二项。第一项与“可能反映偶然”相反，第三、四项明显与常识和原文矛盾。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Science is unreliable because its results are always uncertain
Publishing only successes is the best way to preserve confidence
A record limited to successes weakens a field's ability to test itself
Failures have little to do with scientific progress
questions.explain: 末段说科学之所以有效，是因为错误最终能被发现，而这需要把失败也记录在案；只发表胜利的领域会慢慢失去自我检验的能力，故选第三项。第一项误读“结果并非总是正确”，第二、四项与原文相反。

items.title: Why Small Public Spaces Matter
items.passage:
City planners once paid most attention to large parks and grand squares. These places are important, but they are not the whole story. A small public space at the end of a street can matter just as much to the people who live nearby. A few benches, a little shade, and a place to sit can turn an empty corner into a spot where neighbors meet.

Small spaces work best when they are easy to reach. Most people will not walk far for a short rest, so a tiny garden near a bus stop may be used more often than a large park across town. Older residents, parents with young children, and workers on a lunch break all benefit from places that fit easily into their day.

Comfort is a practical matter. Shade in summer, shelter from rain, and seats at the right height make a space usable across the seasons. Lighting matters too, because a place that feels pleasant in daylight may feel unsafe after dark. Good design is therefore less about costly statues than about small decisions that show someone has thought about how people will sit and wait.

Such spaces also support community life. When people see the same faces regularly, they begin to recognize one another, and that recognition can make a neighborhood feel more friendly and safer. This does not happen automatically; a space must be cared for, and it helps if local people have some say in how it is managed.

The lesson is simple. Cities often measure their success by large projects, but daily life is shaped mostly by small ones. A bench in the right place costs little and is used every day. Paying attention to these modest spaces is one of the least dramatic ways to improve urban life.

questions.q: What does the author say about large parks and squares?
options: They are unimportant compared with small gardens
They are important, but they are not the whole story
They should be replaced by seats at bus stops
They are used mainly by visitors from other cities
questions.explain: 首段承认大公园很重要，但“并非全部”，小型公共空间同样重要，故选第二项。第一项贬低了大公园的作用，第三项文中无此建议，第四项未提及。

questions.q: Why may a tiny garden near a bus stop be used more often than a large park?
options: It is usually cleaner and more beautiful
It offers more sports facilities
It fits easily into people's daily routes
It is open for longer hours
questions.explain: 第二段说人们不会为短暂休息走很远，因此靠近公交站的小花园比城另一头的大公园更常被使用，即它融入日常路线，故选第三项。其余三项文中均未提及。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, what matters most in the design of small spaces?
options: Practical comfort such as shade, seating, and lighting
Expensive statues in the center
Very large fountains and pools
Tall buildings around the space
questions.explain: 第三段强调遮阴、避雨、合适高度的座椅与照明，并说好设计“不在于昂贵的雕像”，故选第一项。第二项被原文否定，第三、四项无据。

questions.q: The word "modest" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: expensive to build
crowded and noisy
famous among planners
small in scale and not impressive
questions.explain: 本段与“大型项目”对比，说长椅成本低却每天被使用，故 modest 指“规模小、不起眼”，与第四项相符。其余三项与上下文相反或无关。

questions.q: What can be inferred about community life in small spaces?
options: It develops automatically once a space is built
It depends entirely on large public budgets
It grows when people meet regularly and have some control over the space
It mainly benefits older residents
questions.explain: 第四段说熟悉的面孔带来相互识别，使社区更友好安全，但强调这“不会自动发生”，需要维护并让本地人参与管理，故选第三项。第一项被原文否定，第二项与“成本低”相反，第四项缩小了受益人群。

items.title: The Price of Speed in News
items.passage:
News used to arrive with delay. A report would be checked, edited, printed or broadcast, and only then reach its audience. The delay was often frustrating, but it had a use: it created a space in which errors could be caught. Today that space has narrowed, and in some cases it has disappeared. The first version of a story may reach readers within moments of an event, long before anyone has had time to confirm what happened.

Speed is not in itself a fault. In a crisis, timely information can save lives, and audiences reasonably expect to hear about important events quickly. The difficulty is that speed and accuracy pull in different directions. Verification takes time: a claim must be traced to a source, a document checked, a photograph examined. Every one of those steps can be skipped, and skipping them is invisible to the reader.

Competition sharpens the temptation. When attention is scarce, being first attracts readers, and a correction rarely travels as far as the original error. Journalists know this, which is why many newsrooms have built habits that protect the checking process: two sources for a serious claim, a separate editor to review a sensitive story, and clear rules about what may be published on the basis of a single message.

The audience has a part to play as well. Readers who reward speed with clicks and shares encourage the behavior they complain about. Slower, explanatory journalism is expensive to produce and easy to ignore, yet it is often what people claim to want. There is a mismatch between what audiences say they value and what their attention actually supports.

None of this is an argument for sluggishness. It is an argument for making the trade-off explicit. A newsroom that says "we will be quick, but we will not publish an unverified claim" is making a promise that can be judged. Speed with visible limits is more honest than speed presented as accuracy.

questions.q: What can be inferred about delay in news reporting in the past?
options: It was always harmful to the public
It made newspapers less interesting to read
It provided a chance to catch errors before publication
It was created mainly by government rules
questions.explain: 首段说过去的延迟虽有不便，却“有用处”：它创造了一个可以抓出错误的空间，故选第三项。第一项与原文相反，第二、四项无据。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what makes verification difficult?
options: It takes time, and its steps can be skipped without readers noticing
It requires technology that most newsrooms lack
It is impossible to carry out during a crisis
It slows down the printing of newspapers
questions.explain: 第二段说核实时要追溯来源、查文件、看照片，每一步都可被跳过且读者看不见，故第一项正确。第二项无据，第三项只涉及危机中的时效，第四项与“印刷”无关。

questions.q: Which practice does the passage mention as protecting accuracy?
options: Publishing a story on the basis of a single message
Removing corrections after a story is updated
Sharing every rumor as soon as it appears
Requiring two sources for a serious claim
questions.explain: 第三段列举新闻编辑室的核查习惯：重大指控要有两个来源、敏感报道需独立编辑复核等，故选第四项。第一项恰是规则要约束的做法，第二、三项与核查精神相反。

questions.q: The word "sluggishness" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: carelessness about facts
slowness in reporting
dishonesty toward readers
silence about mistakes
questions.explain: 末段开头澄清作者并非主张新闻“迟缓”，而是主张把取舍讲清楚，故该词指“缓慢”。第一、三、四项分别指粗心、不诚实与沉默，均非该词含义。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about audience behavior?
options: Readers always prefer slower, explanatory journalism
Clicks and shares have no effect on newsroom choices
What readers reward with attention may conflict with what they say they value
Audiences are unable to judge whether a report is accurate
questions.explain: 第四段指出读者用点击和分享奖励速度，反而鼓励了他们所抱怨的做法，说明“口头上重视的”与“注意力实际支持的”存在错位，故选第三项。第一项与“容易忽视深度报道”矛盾，第二项与“竞争加剧诱惑”相反，第四项过度绝对。

items.title: The Power of Small Habits
items.passage:
People who try to change a habit often begin with a large promise. They plan to exercise every morning, read more, or stop checking a phone at night. Such resolutions express genuine intention, yet many collapse within weeks. The failure is usually not a lack of willpower. It is more often a mismatch between the size of the plan and the ordinary conditions of daily life.

Research on habits suggests that repetition in a stable context is what makes behavior automatic. A habit is not merely a decision repeated; it becomes linked to a cue, such as a time of day, a place, or an action that comes before it. Once the link is strong, the behavior can unfold with little conscious effort. This is why so much advice focuses on designing cues rather than on summoning motivation.

Small steps have an advantage here. A modest action is easy to repeat, and repetition is what builds the link. Someone who intends to walk for a few minutes after lunch is more likely to do it consistently than someone who plans an hour at a gym. Consistency, in turn, produces the sense of identity that sustains habits: people who see themselves as someone who walks tend to keep walking.

The environment can quietly help or hinder. Leaving a book where it will be seen, or placing shoes by the door, reduces the effort required at the moment of decision. Conversely, a habit that depends on constant self-control is fragile, because attention and energy vary from day to day. Relying on willpower alone is a plan with a single point of failure.

Setbacks are normal and need not end a habit. The useful response is to resume quickly rather than to treat a missed day as proof of failure. A habit is better understood as a path that is followed most of the time, not as a perfect record. This gentler standard is easier to live with, and therefore easier to maintain.

questions.q: Why do many resolutions fail, according to the author?
options: The plans are too large for the ordinary conditions of daily life
People today lack willpower almost completely
Habits cannot really be changed once they are formed
People expect results too slowly to stay interested
questions.explain: 首段明确说失败通常不是意志力不足，而是计划规模与日常生活条件不匹配，故选第一项。第二项被作者否定，第三项过于绝对，第四项文中未提。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what makes behavior automatic?
options: Strong motivation at the start
Occasional rewards after success
Repeated action linked to a stable cue
Competition with other people
questions.explain: 第二段说在稳定情境中重复才会使行为自动化，行为与时间、地点等线索建立联系，故选第三项。第一项恰是作者认为不够的观点，第二、四项文中未提。

questions.q: The word "fragile" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: long-lasting and stable
easily disturbed and likely to break down
expensive to maintain
rarely noticed by other people
questions.explain: 本句说依赖持续自控的习惯是 fragile 的，因为注意力与精力每天都不同，故指“脆弱、容易被打断”。第一项与语义相反，第三、四项与语境无关。

questions.q: Why does the author mention placing shoes by the door?
options: To show that exercise requires special equipment
To suggest that tidy homes support healthy living
To warn readers against relying on self-control
To illustrate how reducing effort at decision time helps a habit
questions.explain: 第四段用“把书放在显眼处、把鞋放在门口”说明减少决策时刻的阻力有助于习惯，故选第四项。第一项并非举例目的，第二项文中未提整洁，第三项虽有相关意思但举例本身意在“减少阻力”。

questions.q: What does the author recommend after a missed day?
options: Start again with a much larger goal
Treat the miss as proof that the habit is impossible
Resume quickly rather than demand a perfect record
Abandon the habit and choose a different one
questions.explain: 末段说应尽快恢复，而不是把漏掉的一天当作失败的证据，故选第三项。第一项与“小步更易重复”相反，第二、四项都与作者“挫折很正常”的态度矛盾。

items.title: Cooking as a Life Skill
items.passage:
Cooking at home has become less common in many households. Long working hours, cheap prepared meals, and busy evenings all make it easier to buy food than to prepare it. There is nothing wrong with an occasional ready meal. But when cooking disappears from daily life altogether, people lose more than a little free time. They lose a skill that supports health, budget, and independence.

The health argument is simple. When you cook, you decide how much salt, sugar, and oil goes into a dish. You also decide the size of the portion. Restaurant and packaged food is not automatically unhealthy, but it is usually designed to be appealing, which often means richer and saltier than a person would make at home. Cooking is not a guarantee of good eating, but it gives you choices.

Cost is another reason. A simple meal made from basic ingredients is often cheaper than a takeaway meal, especially when it is shared. This does not mean that everyone should buy the same food. Fresh vegetables, beans, rice, eggs, and frozen produce can all form the base of affordable meals, and shopping with a plan reduces waste. Small habits, such as cooking a larger amount and keeping half for the next day, make the effort more practical.

Perhaps most importantly, cooking builds confidence. Someone who can prepare a few reliable dishes is less dependent on other people and on opening hours. This is useful in many situations: when money is short, when the shops are shut, or when someone simply wants to eat well. Learning three or four simple dishes is a good start. Skill grows with use, and the result is a practical kind of freedom.

questions.q: What does the author say about ready meals?
options: They should be completely banned from the home
They are always unhealthy and should be avoided
An occasional one is fine, but relying on them costs valuable skills
They are usually cheaper than cooking at home
questions.explain: 首段说偶尔吃一顿现成餐并无问题，但若烹饪从生活中完全消失，人失去的是健康、预算与独立所需的一项技能，故选第三项。第一、二项过于绝对，第四项与第三段“家常菜常更便宜”相反。

questions.q: What is one health benefit of cooking at home?
options: It removes all sugar from a meal
You control salt, sugar, oil, and portion size
It guarantees a perfectly balanced diet
It proves that restaurant food is always unhealthy
questions.explain: 第二段说下厨时由你决定盐、糖、油的用量与份量，故选第二项。第一项“all”过度，第三项与“不能保证吃得健康”相反，第四项是原文明确否认的说法。

questions.q: Which suggestion about affordable cooking is made in the passage?
options: Plan your shopping and cook larger amounts to use later
Buy only fresh vegetables and never frozen food
Avoid beans and rice because they are expensive
Stop eating out but never cook at home
questions.explain: 第三段建议带着计划购物以减少浪费，并提到一次多做一些留到次日，故选第一项。第二项与“冷冻食材也可以”矛盾，第三项与“豆类米饭可作基础”相反，第四项自相矛盾。

questions.q: The word "reliable" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: expensive to prepare
quick to cook
new and unusual

questions.explain: 此处说会做几道“靠得住”的菜的人更能自立，故 reliable 指“可靠、行之有效”，与第四项相符。第二项看似相关，但作者强调的是稳定可靠而非速度；其余两项无关。

items.title: Making the Bus Feel Reliable
items.passage:
People often talk about public transport as a matter of vehicles: more buses, newer trains, extra routes. These things matter, but they are not what decides whether a service feels dependable. A journey that is predictable is easy to plan. A journey that may take much longer than expected is difficult to build a day around, even if the average travel time is short.

Reliability begins with information. Riders need to know not only when a bus is due but whether that promise can be trusted. Clear signs, simple apps, and announcements in stations help, but the information must be accurate. A screen that confidently shows a bus which is not coming may be worse than no screen at all, because it teaches people to stop planning and start waiting.

The route itself also shapes the experience. A service that goes everywhere is convenient in theory, but a long, winding route is slow and easy to delay. Simpler lines with frequent vehicles and easy changes often serve passengers better, even if a few people must walk a little farther. Comfort is part of reliability too: a crowded vehicle that passes waiting passengers is, from their point of view, a failure.

The final factor is trust. If problems are explained honestly, riders tolerate them more easily. Silence, by contrast, fills the gap with suspicion. A transport system that admits a delay, offers an alternative, and keeps talking to passengers builds a reputation for honesty even on a bad day. That reputation is valuable, because it encourages people to try the service again.

None of these ideas requires a new railway. Many improvements involve better information, clearer routes, and more honest communication. They are unglamorous, but they address what travelers actually experience. A network becomes reliable not only when it moves vehicles, but when it lets people plan with confidence.

questions.q: What do people often think public transport mainly needs?
options: More accurate information for passengers
More vehicles, newer trains, and extra routes
Cheaper tickets and longer opening hours
Better communication during delays
questions.explain: 首段说人们常把公共交通看作车辆问题：更多公交、更新的列车、更多线路，故选第二项。第一、四项是作者后文提出的重点，而非“人们常认为”的内容，第三项文中未提。

questions.q: Why can inaccurate information be worse than no information at all?
options: It costs the transport company a lot of money
It makes drivers and staff angry
It wastes electricity in stations
It teaches people to stop planning and simply wait
questions.explain: 第二段说屏幕 confidently 显示一辆不会来的车，可能比没有屏幕更糟，因为这会让人放弃计划、只是干等，故选第四项。其余三项文中均未提及。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about simple, frequent lines?
options: They can serve passengers better even if some people walk farther
They are always unpopular with local residents
They increase delays on long routes
They should be replaced by routes that go everywhere
questions.explain: 第三段说站点更少、班次更密的简单线路往往更方便，即使少数人要多走一点路，故选第一项。第二项与“往往更好地服务乘客”相反，第三项无据，第四项与作者对“处处都到”的批评矛盾。

questions.q: The word "unglamorous" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: very costly to build
unusual and experimental
not exciting or impressive
dangerous for passengers
questions.explain: 末段说这些改进“不需要新建铁路”，虽不引人注目，却直接改善乘客体验，故指“不起眼、不光鲜”。第一、二、四项与语境不符。

questions.q: What can be inferred about trust in public transport?
options: It is impossible to build once a service is delayed
It depends only on buying new vehicles
It declines whenever information is accurate
Honest communication about problems helps to build it
questions.explain: 第四段说如实解释问题，乘客更容易接受，承认延误并提供替代方案的系统即便在糟糕的日子也能建立诚实的名声，故选第四项。第一项过于绝对，第二项与全文主旨相反，第三项与“准确信息有帮助”矛盾。

P1 The wallet is heading for extinction. As a day-to-day essential, it will die off with the generation who read print newspapers. The kind of shopping where you hand over notes and count out change in return now happens only in the most minor of our retail encounters, like buying a bar of chocolate or a pint of milk, from a corner shop. At the shops where you spend any real money, that money is increasingly abstracted. And this is more and more true, the higher up the scale you go. At the most cutting-edge retail stores Victoria Beckham on Dover Street, for instance you don't go and stand at any kind of cash register, when you decide to pay. The staff are equipped with iPads to take your payment while you relax on a sofa.

P2 Which is nothing more or less than excellent service, if you have the money. But across society, the abstraction of the idea of cash makes me uneasy. Maybe I'm just old-fashioned. But earning money isn't quick or easy for most of us. Isn't it a bit weird that spending it should happen in half a blink(眨眼) of an eye? Doesn't a wallet—that time-honoured Friday-night feeling of pleasing, promising fatness— represent something that matters?

P3 But I'll leave the economics to the experts. What bothers me about the death of the wallet is the change it represents in our physical environment. Everything about the look and feel of a wallet—the way the fastenings and materials wear and tear and loosen with age, the plastic and paper and gold and silver, and handwritten phone numbers and printed cinema tickets—is the very opposite of what our world is becoming. The opposite of a wallet is a smartphone or an iPad. The rounded edges, cool glass, smooth and unknowable as a pebble(鹅卵石). Instead of digging through pieces of paper and peering into corners, we move our fingers left and right. No more counting out coins. Show your wallet, if you still have one. It may not be here much longer.

P1 It's late in the evening: time to close the book and turn off the computer. You're done for the day. What you may not realize, however, is that the learning process actually continues—in your dreams.

P2 It might sound like science fiction, but researchers are increasingly focusing on the relationship between the knowledge and skills our brains absorb during the day and the fragmented, often bizarre imaginings they generate at night. Scientists have found that dreaming about a task we've learned is associated with improved performance in that activity (suggesting that there's some truth to the popular notion that we're "getting" a foreign language once we begin dreaming in it). What's more, researchers are coming to recognize that dreaming is an essential part of understanding, organizing and retaining what we learn.

P3 While we sleep, research indicates, the brain replays the patterns of activity it experienced during waking hours, allowing us to enter what one psychologist calls a neural(神经的) virtual reality. A vivid example of such replay can be seen in a video researchers made recently about sleep disorders. They taught a series of dance moves to a group of patients with conditions like sleepwalking, in which the sleeper engages in the kind of physical movement that does not normally occur during sleep. They then videotaped the subjects as they slept. Lying in bed, eyes closed, one female patient on the tape performs the dance moves she learned earlier.

P4 This shows that while our bodies are at rest, our brains are drawing what's important from the information and events we've recently encountered, then integrating that data into the vast store of what we already know. In a 2010 study, researchers at Harvard Medical School reported that college students who dreamed about a computer maze(迷宫) task they had learned showed a 10-fold improvement in their ability to find their way through the maze compared with participants who did not dream about the task.

P5 Robert Stickgold, one of the Harvard researchers, suggests that studying right before bedtime or taking a nap following a study session in the afternoon might increase the odds of dreaming about the material. Think about that as your head hits the pillow tonight.

P1 Americans spend billions of dollars each year trying to change our weight with diets, gym memberships and plastic surgery.

P2 Trying to live up to the images of "perfect" models and movie heroes has a dark side: anxiety and depression, as well as unhealthy strategies for weight loss or muscle gain. It also has a financial cost. Having an eating disorder boosts annual health care costs by nearly US $2,000 per person.

P3 Why is there both external and internal pressure to look "perfect"? One reason is that society rewards people who are thin and healthy looking. Researchers have shown that body mass index is related to wages and income. Especially for women, there is a clear penalty at work for being overweight or obese. Some studies have also found an impact for men, though a less noticeable one.

P4 While the research literature is clear that labor market success is partly based on how employers and customers perceive your body image, no one had explored the other side of the question. Does a person's own perception of body image matter to earnings and other indicators of success in the workplace?

P5 Our recently published study answered this question by tracking a large national random sample of Americans over a critical time period when bodies change from teenage shape into adult form and when people build their identities.

P6 As in other research, women in our sample tend to over-perceive their weight—they think they're heavier than they are—while men tend to under-perceive theirs.

P8 While the continued gender penalty in the labor market is frustrating, our finding that misperceived weight does not harm workers is more heartening.

P9 Since employers' perception of weight is what matters in the labor market, changing discrimination laws to include body type as a category would also help. Michigan is the only state that prohibits discrimination on the basis of weight and height. We believe expanding such protections would make the labor market more fair and efficient.

P1 The work-life balance is dead. By this, I'm not advocating that you should give up your pursuit of having a fulfilling career and a thriving personal life, and I'm definitely not saying that you have to give up one to have the other. I also acknowledge that we have a work-life problem, but I'm arguing that the concept of balance has never been helpful, because it's too limiting. You see, our language makes a difference, and how we refer to things matters because it affects our thinking and therefore our actions.

P2 At the minimum, most of us work because we want to be able to support ourselves, our families, and the people around us. In the ideal world, we're all doing work that we're proud of and that provides meaning and purpose to us. But even if your job doesn't give you shivers of joy each new day, working is a part of what each of us does and the contribution we make to society. When you separate work and life, it's a little bit harder to make that connection. But when you think of work as part of a full life and a complete experience, it becomes easier to see that success in one aspect often supports another.

P3 Losing your balance and falling isn't pleasant. A goal to balance suggests that things could quickly get off balance, and that causes terrible outcomes. It's more constructive to think of solutions that continue to evolve over shifts in life and work. Rather than falling or failing, you may have good days or better days or not-so-good days. These variations are normal, and it's more useful to think of life as something that is ever evolving and changing, rather than a high-risk enterprise where things could go wrong with one misstep.

P4 How we talk to ourselves matters, and how we talk about issues makes a difference. Let's bury "work-life balance" and think bigger and better about work-life fulfillment to do a little less balancing and a lot more living.

items.passage:
P1 When was cleaning a crime? When you're doing it to create art, obviously. A number of street artists around the world have started expressing themselves through a practice known as reverse graffiti(涂鸦). They find dirty surfaces and paint them with images or messages using cleaning brushes or pressure hoses(高压水管). Either way, it's the same principle: the image is made by cleaning away the dirt. Each artist has their own individual style but all artists share a common aim: to draw attention to the pollution in our cities. The UK's Paul Curtis, better known as Moose, operates around Leeds and London and has been commissioned by a number of companies to make reverse graffiti advertisements.

P2 Brazilian artist, Alexandre Orion, turned one of Sao Paulo's transport tunnels into an amazing wall painting in 2006 by getting rid of the dirt. Made up of a series of white skulls(颅骨), the painting reminds drivers of the effect their pollution is having on the planet. "Every motorist sits in the comfort of their car, but they don't give any consideration to the price their comfort has for the environment and consequently for themselves," says Orion.

P3 The anti-pollution message of the reverse graffiti artists confuses city authorities since the main argument against graffiti is that it spoils the appearance of both types of property: public and private. This was what Leeds City Council said about Moose's work: "Leeds residents want to live in clean and attractive neighbourhoods. We view this kind of advertising as environmental damage and will take strong action against it." Moose was ordered to "clean up his act." How was he supposed to do this: by making all property he had cleaned dirty again?

P4 As for the Brazilian artist's work, the authorities were annoyed but could find nothing to charge him with. They had no other option but to clean the tunnel—but only the parts Alexandre had already cleaned. The artist merely continued his campaign on the other side. The city officials then decided to take drastic action. They not only cleaned the whole tunnel but every tunnel in Sao Paulo.

items.passage:
P1 The practice of paying children an allowance became popular in America about 100 years ago. Nowadays, American kids on average receive about $800 per year in allowance. But the vast majority of American parents who pay allowance tie it to the completion of housework. Although many parents believe that paying an allowance for completing chores benefits their children, a range of experts expressed concern that tying allowance very closely to chores may not be ideal. In fact, the way chores work in many households worldwide points to another way.

P2 Suniya Luthar, a psychologist, is against paying kids for chores. Luthar is not opposed to giving allowances, but she thinks it's important to establish that chores are done not because they will lead to payment, but because they keep the household running. Luthar's suggested approach to allowance is compatible with that of writer Ron Lieber, who advises that allowances be used as a means of showing children how to save, give, and spend on things they care about. Kids should do chores, he writes, "for the same reason adults do, because the chores need to be done, and not with the expectation of compensation."

P3 This argument has its critics, but considering the way chores are undertaken around the world may change people's thinking. Professor David Lancy of Utah State University has studied how families around the world handle chores. At about 18 months of age, Lancy says, most children become eager to help their parents, and in many cultures, they begin helping with housework at that age. They begin with very simple tasks, but their responsibilities gradually increase. And they do these tasks without payment. Lancy contrasts this with what happens in America. "We deny our children's bids to help until they are 6 or 7 years old," Lancy says, "when many have lost the desire to help and then try to motivate them with payment. The solution to this problem is not to try to use money as an incentive to do housework, but to get children involved in housework much earlier, when they actually want to do it."

items.passage:
P1 Picture this: You're at a movie theater food stand loading up on snacks. You have a choice of a small, medium or large soda. The small is $3.50 and the large is $5.50. It's a tough decision: The small size may not last you through the whole movie, but $5.50 for some sugary drink seems ridiculous. But there's a third option, a medium soda for $5.25. Medium may be the perfect amount of soda for you, but the large is only a quarter more. If you're like most people, you end up buying the large (and taking a bathroom break midshow).

P2 If you're wondering who would buy the medium soda, the answer is almost no one. In fact, there's a good chance the marketing department purposely priced the medium soda as a decoy(诱饵), making you more likely to buy the large soda rather than the small.

P3 I have written about this peculiarity in human nature before with my friend Dan Ariely, who studied this phenomenon extensively after noticing pricing for subscriptions(订阅) to The Economist. The digital subscription was $59, the print subscription was $125, and the print plus digital subscription was also $125. No one in their right mind would buy the print subscription when you could get digital as well for the same price, so why was it even an option? Ariely ran an experiment and found that when only the two "real" choices were offered, more people chose the less-expensive digital subscription. But the addition of the bad option made people much more likely to choose the more expensive print plus digital option.

P4 Brain scientists call this effect "asymmetric dominance" and it means that people gravitate toward the choice nearest a clearly inferior option. Marketing professors call it the decoy effect, which is certainly easier to remember. Lucky for consumers, almost no one in the business community understands it.

P5 The decoy effect works because of the way our brains assign value when making choices. Value is almost never absolute; rather, we decide an object's value relative to our other choices. If more options are introduced, the value equation changes.
